question: to the Commission Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI) Subject:

The largest steel plant in Romania, formerly Sidex Galați, was purchased by ArcelorMittal in 2001 and taken over by the Liberty House Group (GFG Alliance) in 2019, and is the most important steel producing site in Romania. The plant is currently in an arrangement with creditors and a restructuring plan has been implemented. It is a key industrial and geostrategic pillar for Romania and South-East Europe, with even greater strategic relevance in the current geopolitical climate marked by the war in Ukraine and the need to strengthen Europe’s steel supply chains. The plant has a vital role to play for the European Union’s defence industry, infrastructure and strategic autonomy. Its location in proximity to Ukraine lends it additional importance from the perspective of the reconstruction of the region and the reconfiguration of industrial chains. Given the challenges faced by the steel industry and the dependence on external markets, rescuing and developing this industrial site constitutes a strategic priority for the European Union. 1.
Have the Romanian authorities contacted the Commission to request support for the development of this plant, given its strategic and geopolitical importance?
What tools and possibilities does the Commission have at its disposal to support the development of the plant and prevent the loss of specialists and skilled workers?
Is it possible to draw up, as a matter of urgency, an EU-level plan for the development and support of this strategic industrial objective?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.4.2026) The European Steel and Metals Action Plan1, adopted on 19 March 2025, outlines a roadmap to help secure the industry’s competitiveness and support its decarbonisation. To this end, policy instruments and initiatives available or forthcoming include: Trade defence instruments on unfair pricing, subsidies for the steel sector, and tariffrate quotas on EU steel imports. The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism keeping carbon costs of imported steel comparable to those of EU producers; Funding for low-carbon steel technologies under the European Green Deal; The Industrial Accelerator Act2 to help boost manufacturing, grow businesses, and create jobs; Amendments to the European Social Fund Plus and the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund, as well as the Pact for Skills3 support workers, companies affected by structural change, and large-scale partnerships of energy-intensive industries; The Emissions Trading System State aid Guidelines4, the Clean Industrial Deal State aid Framework5, and the Guidelines on State aid for climate, environmental protection and energy6 support decarbonisation plant development. The General Block Exemption Regulation7 helps retain skilled staff during plant transformation. Besides, Romania listed the Liberty Galati plant under the Romanian Just Transition Programme. Its funding contributes to the steel industry’s transition towards clean and efficient technologies, including training and re-skilling of staff. These measures show the Commission's commitment to support the steel industry. Without prejudice to other EU law obligations, they can be tailored to specific strategic industrial needs. The Commission is also ready to discuss any planned measures by Romania under EU competition rules.
